data.copy:
My neighbor made coffee on his back porch at sunrise for 26 years. Every morning. 6:10 AM. Same blue mug. Same old metal patio chair. Same little radio playing the local news just loud enough for me to hear it through my kitchen window.

Then one morning, nothing.

Just birds.

I stood at my sink rinsing a cereal bowl and waited for the sound of his screen door.

It didn’t come.

No chair scraping against the concrete.

No radio static.

No spoon tapping against the mug.

No Earl coughing twice before taking that first sip.

I know how strange this sounds.

But when a sound has been part of your life for decades, you know when it’s missing.

Something was wrong with Earl.

My name is Karen.

I’m 57.

I’ve lived in the same brick ranch on Linden Street in Greensboro, North Carolina for 22 years.

My husband Dale and I moved in the summer of 2003 with two kids, a dog, and a leaky water heater.

The kids are grown now.

The dog is buried under the dogwood out back.

The water heater finally gave up last March.

But Earl was always there.

Earl Whitaker.

68 years old.

Retired postal carrier.

Lived in the white split-level next door with his wife Marlene and a Labrador named Biscuit, who used to come over and eat my tomatoes off the vine before I could pick them.

Earl made coffee on that porch because, in his words:

“Morning belongs outside. Anybody drinking coffee indoors before July is wasting daylight.”

He’d been doing it for 26 years.

Six-ten in the morning.

Screen door.

Chair scrape.

Radio.

Coffee spoon.

Same routine.

More reliable than my coffee maker.

More reliable than my husband’s snoring.

More reliable than my own kids calling on Sunday.

You don’t realize how much you count on something until it stops.

The first morning Earl didn’t come out, I told myself he was sleeping in.

He’d earned it.

The second morning, I told myself maybe he and Marlene were visiting their daughter in Raleigh.

data.copy: The terrible truth I learned on my chiropractor's table is that for a man who sits for a living, a $400 ergonomic chair is worth about as much as a lawn chair. As we push through our 40s, our spines lose their natural shock absorbers, and every hour in a "good" office chair is slowly crushing the nerves we depend on. My failure to understand this simple principle of anatomy is why I spent $2,800 on chairs that didn't work, and why I ended up on a neurologist's exam table, unable to feel my own left foot.My name is Mark. I'm 47. I used to be the guy who ran 10Ks on weekends and played pickup basketball on Thursdays. I built a career as a senior software architect — eleven hours a day at my desk, most of it in back-to-back meetings. And for the last two years, since we went permanent remote, my life has followed a script. "How's work, Mark?" "Fine. Just tired." But I wasn't fine. A deep, burning ache had taken up residence in my lower back and right hip. It shot down my leg like an electric wire every time I stood up from my desk. A part of me — the part that's still an athlete — knew something was seriously wrong. But I was a man in his 40s with a demanding job. Back pain was just the tax you paid.I tried to fix it. God, I tried. I bought the $800 mesh chair everyone on LinkedIn was raving about. Used it for three weeks. No change. I bought a lumbar pillow, the memory foam kind with the adjustable strap. It molded to my back and then just... stopped doing anything. I bought a standing desk converter. Standing made it worse. Every legitimate attempt to fix myself failed, and I started to believe this was just my new life. I started taking ibuprofen like vitamins. I told myself I was getting older. I told myself it would pass.It didn't.Then, on a Wednesday morning at 8:40 AM, during a client presentation, it happened. I Declined Blood Pressure Medication for 3 Years. Here's What Happened to My Heart Health.

I've been a nurse for 38 years, and high blood pressure is one of the hardest things I see patients struggle with. The morning headaches. The dizzy spells when you stand up. That pounding in your chest that never stops. I've had patients tell me they wake up at 3 AM feeling their heart racing. Day and night, it never stops.

About three years ago, it happened to me. My own blood pressure started climbing out of control. I have hypertension. All those years of long shifts and not taking care of myself the way I should have finally caught up with me.

At first it was just feeling lightheaded when I stood up. Then came the headaches. Those throbbing morning headaches that hit you the second you wake up. By the end of my shift, I could feel my heart pounding in my chest. But the worst part? Nighttime. The second I'd finally fall asleep, I'd wake up at 3 AM with my heart racing. Again. And again. I'd be laying there feeling my pulse throbbing in my neck, scared and exhausted no matter how much rest I tried to get. I'd be up half the night trying to calm down between episodes.

Now I was the one living with it. And let me tell you, every patient was right. It's a living hell.

My doctor offered me blood pressure medication. I smiled politely and said I'd think about it.

data.caption: The collar worked until she learned to tilt her head
data.copy:
I used to think dog training was about willpower.
 
The dog's willpower. My willpower. Whether I was consistent enough, patient enough, firm enough. Whether the dog was smart enough, stubborn enough, motivated enough.
 
After two years of dealing with my dog Max and his barking, and after buying what I can only describe as an embarrassing collection of devices and programs that did nothing useful, I learned that I had been thinking about this completely wrong.
 
If you have bought a device that worked for ten days and then stopped working, this is for you. If you have had a trainer tell you your dog needs months of consistency while your neighbor is filing complaints this week, this is for you. If you have stood in a pet store aisle reading box descriptions and suspected that none of them were going to work, you were right, and I want to explain exactly why.
 
Max is a four-year-old Belgian Malinois mix. If you know the breed, you already understand the baseline energy level. If you do not know the breed, imagine a dog that was designed by someone who thought German Shepherds were a little too relaxed.
 
He is brilliant and loyal and completely impossible to settle down when something catches his attention. And when Max decided something was worth barking at, which was everything that moved within range of our fence, he committed. Long sustained bursts. Not the two barks and done that you read about in dog training articles. Full episodes that could go five, ten minutes before whatever triggered him moved out of range.
 
I am a person who works from home. I have a client that pays me for clear audio on regular calls. I have neighbors who have been patient for two years and were starting to run out of patience. And I have a dog who I love and did not want to live in conflict with.
 
I tried the obvious things first.
 
Dog behavior is not about willpower. It is about biology.

data.caption: It's not "just reflux"
data.copy:
What Your Doctor Calls "Just Reflux" On 0zempic Is Almost Always Misdiagnosed

Sometime in the last six months, you sat across from your doctor and described a problem.

You were waking up in the middle of the night choking. Or coughing. Or feeling like there was a burning taste in the back of your throat. You told her you had been on 0zempic for a few months (or a year, or two) and the symptoms had started somewhere along the way.

She looked at her chart for about thirty seconds. Then she said some version of this: "It is probably just reflux. We see it sometimes with these medications. Let's try Pri1osec."

That is the conversation millions of GLP-1 patients have been having. And that diagnosis (let's call it "just reflux") is the reason most of them are still suffering.

Because what you have is not just reflux. What you have has a clinical name. It shows up routinely in long-term users of these medications. Roughly 1 in 7 develop it. And the treatment your doctor prescribed is, statistically, almost guaranteed to fail.

The reason it will fail is not because you have unusually severe reflux, or because the dose was too low, or because you did not raise the head of your bed high enough. It will fail because acid is not the actual mechanism. The label is right about the symptom. It is wrong about the cause.

---

I know how this sounds. If there were a documented pattern that was being misdiagnosed on a massive scale, somebody would have made a fuss about it by now. There would be a class action. There would be a New York Times piece.

But that is not how new prescription reactions move through the medical system. They get reported. They get published in specialty journals that most family doctors never read. The standard of care lags the literature by anywhere from two to ten years.

data.copy:
The very first prophecy in the entire Bible was spoken in a garden, minutes after the world broke.
Most Christians have read it dozens of times.
Almost none of them know it is there.

Every Christian knows the story of Genesis 3.

The serpent. The fruit. The fall. God discovers what has happened. He confronts Adam and Eve. And then He curses the serpent.

That is where most people stop paying attention.

Because what God says next is the most important sentence in the entire Old Testament. And it is hiding inside what looks like a curse on a snake.

"I will put enmity between you and the woman, and between your offspring and hers. He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel."

That is Genesis 3:15.

Theologians call it the Protoevangelium. The first gospel. The first announcement of Jesus in all of Scripture.

Spoken in a garden. Before Abraham. Before Moses. Before David. Before any prophet ever lived. Before the first consequence of the fall had even landed.

And most Christians have read it their entire lives without ever being told what it actually says.

Look at the details.

"Her offspring."

In ancient Hebrew, lineage was always traced through the father. Always. Every genealogy in the Old Testament runs through the male line. The son of Abraham. The son of Isaac. The son of Jacob. The son of David.

But Genesis 3:15 says "her offspring." The woman's seed.

That is the only place in the entire Old Testament where offspring is traced through a woman instead of a man.

Scholars have debated this grammatical anomaly for three thousand years. It breaks every convention of ancient Hebrew lineage tracking.

Unless the child has no human father.

The virgin birth. Predicted in the third chapter of the first book. Hidden inside a single pronoun.

Now look at the injuries.

"He will crush your head, and you will strike his heel."

Two injuries. Two different severities.

The serpent strikes the heel. Painful. Bloody. But survivable. A wound that hurts but do…

data.copy:
Ich bin alleinerziehende Mutter mit zwei Kindern — und alle haben gelacht, als ich den Hund adoptiert habe, der jeden angesprungen hat, der näher als drei Meter kam.
Sie sagten, ich sei überfordert.
Zu beschäftigt.
„Deine Kinder werden gebissen."
„Sie ist bis Montag wieder im Tierheim," flüsterten sie.
Das war vor vier Monaten.
Seit Tag vier kein einziger aggressiver Vorfall.
Jetzt läuft sie jeden Samstag ruhig mit meinen Kindern über den Wochenmarkt.
Und was die Reaktivität gestoppt hat, brauchte null Training, null Maulkorb — und genau 72 Stunden.

Die Koordinatorin des Tierheims legte ihre Hand auf meinen Arm.
„Jennifer. Bitte. Denk darüber nach."
Sie zeigte auf die Kennkarte.
Große rote Buchstaben: „RÜCKGABE #4 – LETZTE ADOPTION"
Darunter geschrieben:
„Springt Menschen auf Spaziergängen an" „Hat 2 Wohnungen aus Angst zerstört" „Hat 3 verschiedene Trainer bei Bewertungen attackiert" „Barriereaggression – extrem"
„Vier Familien konnten sie nicht halten," sagte sie vorsichtig. „Alle hatten Erfahrung mit reaktiven Hunden. Sie hat jeden einzelnen Menschen angesprungen."
Ihre Augen wanderten zu meinen zwei Kindern, die in der Lobby warteten.
„Du hast Kinder. Allein. Dieser Hund hat sich noch nie erfolgreich in ein häusliches Umfeld integriert."
Ich schaute den Hund an.
Sasha. Vierjähriger Schäferhundmischling.
Lief im Käfig auf und ab.
Sprang gegen das Gitter, jedes Mal wenn jemand vorbeiging.
Augen voller Panik.
Diesen Blick erkannte ich sofort.
Ich hatte ihn nach meiner Scheidung in meinem eigenen Gesicht gesehen.
Das war kein böser Hund.
Das war ein verängstigter Hund.
„Ich nehme sie," sagte ich.
Die Mitarbeiter tauschten Blicke aus.
Eine Freiwillige flüsterte der anderen zu.
„Sie hält keine drei Tage durch."
„Beim ersten Anspringen eines der Kinder ist sie fertig."
Die Koordinatorin räusperte sich.
Ihre Stimme wurde leise.

I picked up my clothes off his floor

Sat in the back seat terrified the driver would smell it too

data.caption: It's not "just reflux"
data.copy:
1 In 7 Female GLP-1 Users Are Choking In Their Sleep — And Being Told It's "Minor Reflux"

Approximately 14.5% of patients on GLP-1 medications (Ozempic, Mounjaro, Wegovy, Zepbound, and Rybelsus) develop a documented respiratory side effect that is being systematically misdiagnosed by primary care doctors across the country.

That is roughly 1 in every 7 users.

The clinical term for it is "nasopharyngitis." That language has appeared in the post-market adverse event reporting since these drugs went mainstream. The actual experience of it is this: waking up at 3 AM choking on what feels like acid pouring into your windpipe, gasping for air, coughing, sometimes aspirating liquid into your lungs while you sleep.

When patients describe this to their family doctors, they are told it is "minor reflux." They are prescribed Prilosec or Nexium. They are told to elevate the head of their bed, lose more weight, and not eat after 6 PM. And when none of that stops the 3 AM episodes, they are told to keep trying.

It is not minor reflux.

It is not reflux in the way the medical establishment has been treating reflux for the last forty years. It is a documented inflammatory cascade running from the gut to the lungs, and it does not respond to acid suppression because the problem was never acid.

And while the clinical literature catches up to what is actually happening, roughly 1 in 7 GLP-1 users are choking themselves awake at 3 AM and being told there is nothing serious going on.

Women in particular are getting the worst end of this. Not because they are physiologically more susceptible (though emerging data suggests they may be), but because women's symptoms are statistically more likely to be dismissed as anxiety, "just stress," or "just minor" in primary care visits. So the women in this group are not only living through it, they are being told over and over that they are imagining it.

data.caption: Die Tochter meines Nachbarn wurde im letzten September von meinem Hund gebissen. Ich poste das, weil mir niemand den wahren Grund gesagt hat.
data.copy:
Ich will diesen Post nicht schreiben.

Aber ich sehe immer wieder Menschen in Gruppen für reaktive Hunde, die genau das durchmachen, was ich durchgemacht habe — Tausende für Trainer ausgeben, alles richtig machen, zusehen wie ihre Hunde schlimmer werden — und ich kann nicht mehr schweigen.

Mein Hund Finn hat im letzten September die neunjährige Tochter meines Nachbarn gebissen.

Ihr ging es gut. Oberflächlich. Brauchte nicht mal Nähte.

Aber Finn musste beurteilt werden. Mein Nachbar hätte Anzeige erstatten können. Das Ordnungsamt wurde eingeschaltet.

Ich verbrachte drei Wochen damit, nicht zu wissen, ob ich ihn verlieren würde.

Ich bin Tom. Finn ist ein 5-jähriger Rettungs-Border-Collie-Mischling. Ich habe ihn seit er 18 Monate alt war, als er aus einer Weitervermittlungssituation mit dokumentierter Leinenreaktivitätsgeschichte zu mir kam.

Ich wusste, worauf ich mich einließ.

Oder ich dachte, ich wüsste es.

Zweieinhalb Jahre lang tat ich alles, was die Reaktivhunde-Community einem sagt.

Ich fand innerhalb des ersten Monats einen zertifizierten Verhaltensspezialisten. Wir arbeiteten acht Monate zusammen. Echte Fortschritte — Finns Schwelle ging von 50 Metern auf etwa 20 Meter, bevor er reagierte. Ich dachte, wir kämen ans Ziel.

Dann zog sein bisheriger Verhaltensspezialist weg und wir fingen mit einem neuen an.

Neue Ansätze. Bei manchen Dingen mehr Fortschritt, bei anderen Rückschritte. Seine Schwelle war inkonsistent — manche Tage super, manche Tage schrecklich, kein klares Muster.

Ich engagierte eine dritte Trainerin, die sich speziell auf Beißprävention und Leinenreaktivität spezialisiert hatte. Sie war ausgezeichnet. Geduldig, kompetent, freundlich mit Finn.

Wir arbeiteten sechs Monate mit ihr.

Finn konnte die meisten Tage an Hunden auf der gegenüberliegenden Straßenseite vorbeigehen.

Aber „die meisten Tage" reichte nicht. Und ich verstand nie wirklich, warum manche Tage gut und manche katastrophal waren.

data.caption: The MRI Came Back Fine. The Pain Didn't.
data.copy:
"Honey, you're just overweight. Lose ten pounds and come back."

That's what my doctor said when I told him I couldn't make it through a school day without sitting on my desk.

I'm a high school biology teacher. I'm 48. I've been on my feet six periods a day on hard tile floors for sixteen years. My right hip has been getting worse for two years.

If you're a woman in your 40s, 50s, or 60s and your hip has been hurting longer than you want to admit, this is for you.

If you've tried cortisone shots, physical therapy, glucosamine, turmeric, collagen in your morning coffee, Voltaren, Tiger Balm, heating pads, foam rollers, a TENS unit that lives in your nightstand, and a pillow between your knees every single night, and you are still hurting...

This is for you.

Especially if they keep treating your hip like it's just a bad joint, but nothing actually changes.

I want to tell you what nobody told me in any of those appointments. And I want to tell you why I think they missed it.

You are not doing anything wrong. The bowls were never the problem. And every time you scrub that chin, you are making it worse.

Feline acne. Tiny blackheads forming at the base of the hair follicles. Common. Manageable. Nothing to worry about.

data.copy:
If your cat has a dry hacking cough that won't stop.

If you've tried the hairball gel, the antibiotics, the prescription food.

If your vet keeps saying hairballs while the cough keeps getting worse.

You are not dealing with a hairball problem.

You are dealing with a heart that is starving for the one nutrient your cat's food has been destroying before it ever reaches her bowl.

I know because I watched Pepper cough for six months before I found out what was actually happening.

Two vets never mentioned it once.

Not because they didn't know.

Because they did.

My name is Anna Rodriguez. I live in Tampa with my cat Pepper.

So let me tell you what happened with her, because her story is gonna open your eyes to how messed up this really is.

For MONTHS, and I mean like six straight months, Pepper was slowly dying right in front of me.

It started with the cough. Dry hacking cough. Like she was trying to bring up a hairball but nothing was coming up.

She'd crouch down low. Stretch her neck out. Make this awful gagging sound. Then nothing.

At first it was once or twice a day. Annoying but I could ignore it.

Then it crept into the nights.

The first night it happened, I woke up around 3 AM thinking someone was choking in my apartment. That was the sound. Like someone choking.

But it was just Pepper. On the bed next to me. Hacking.

The next night it happened twice. Then three times. Then it just never stopped.

She'd cough so hard her whole little body would shake. Then go quiet for five minutes. Then start again.

By the second week, she was coughing so much I honestly couldn't count how many times she did it. It was constant.

I'd watch her in the morning and her eyes looked tired. Like she'd been up all night fighting something.

Because she had been.

So obviously, I take her to the vet, right?

Multiple vets. Different clinics. We're talking $14 hairball gel, $280 in antibiotics, weeks of pills hidden in treats, the whole nine yards.

And you know what ever…

keyword.description: Free-text search string (lowercased server-side). Use for product names, brands, hooks, domains — not for category/niche (use niches).
keyword.allowed_values: Any string; empty = no text filter.

searchkeyword.description: Which ad field keyword searches. NOT a niche/category selector.
searchkeyword.allowed_values: All, landingurl, pagename, adtext, productname. Default All when keyword is set.

countries.description: Ad target countries (where the ad runs — wlads.countries). Not store HQ.
countries.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.
countries.notes: MX/CO/CL are not in this Meta targeting catalog. Use store_based_in for stores based in those markets.

excludeCountries.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2: US, GB, DK, NL, BE, IE, NO, SE, FR, DE, IT, CA, NZ, AU, BR, AT, CH, ES, FI, PL, PT, GR, TR, AE, SA, QA, KW, BH, OM, JO, IL, LB, IQ, EG.

storebasedin.description: Store Based In (dashboard storebasedin → store_traffic.shop_origin_country). Use for Mexico/Colombia/Chile/etc. store HQ.
storebasedin.allowed_values: Comma-separated ISO2 including MX, CO, CL, AR, PE and other Explore Shops Based In markets.

niches.description: Product category / vertical filter (dashboard Meta niches). Use when user asks for a category, niche, vertical, or market — not keyword.
niches.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: CG, AM, GG, JY, GS, HT, BY, BG, SK, WC, MC, SP, KS, TS, HE, PS, DP, HI, FT, OG, OP, TR, AC, AA, BM, FK, SH, SW, EL, FW, WT, EW, FR, GM, PH, EC, WE, SC, BE, MU, PA, CB, CF, CP, DC, CT, HH, SG, YG, CC, PZ, LS, GP, WN, SF, OR, MG, PB. See allowed_niches in response for code→label map. Fashion/clothing = CG.

website.description: Detected store/checkout technology on the landing page (dashboard Website filter).
website.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated codes: SH, TP, BU, LS, CC, SL, TA, GG, FU, CS, LP, FO, SI, GP, XS, YC, HY, DI, MS, SB, PP, WC, TT, TW, PI, GO, SC, FB, MG, WP, SQ, PS, GM, KV, CO, HJ, WX, AR, BC, MC. SH=Shopify, WC=WooCommerce, CS=Clickfunnels. See allowed_technologies in response.

languages.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

excludeLanguages.allowed_values: Comma-separated: en, nl, de, no, fr, sv, da, it, pt, es, fi, pl, tr, ar, he.

apps.description: Shopify apps detected on the store.
apps.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated app names/ids from dashboard Apps filter. See allowed_apps in response.

excludeApps.description: Exclude stores using these Shopify apps.
excludeApps.allowed_values: Comma-separated app names/ids. See allowed_apps in response.

themes.description: Shopify theme name on the store (exact match).
themes.allowed_values: All, or comma-separated exact theme names from dashboard Themes filter (discover via GET /api/themes).

scaling.allowed_values: rising, stable, declining, nodownscaling, upscaling, downscaling.

mediafilter.allowed_values: videos, images, carousel, dco. Omit/All = all formats.

pagetypefilter.allowed_values: products, collections, funnels, nofunnels. Empty/All = all types.

adscorefilter.description: WinningHunter ad score tier (Established / Has Potential / Unestablished).
adscorefilter.allowed_values: winning (Established), scaling (Has Potential), testing (Unestablished). Requires matching account tier.

lowimpressions.description: Hide ads with very low impressions.
lowimpressions.allowed_values: hide (exclude low-impression rows). Omit = show all.

rankgrowthfilter.description: Within-brand ad rank momentum vs historic rank_history.
rankgrowthfilter.allowed_values: Comma-separated subset of: rising, stable, declining.

minadrank.description: Minimum within-brand ad rank (lower rank number = stronger ad for that brand, e.g. #1).

min.description: Minimum duplicate/active-seen ad count on the page.

minactiveads.description: Minimum active Meta ads on the advertiser Facebook page (total_active_ads_on_page).
minactiveads.notes: find_winning_products auto-applies minactiveads=50 for US when not set (see forced block).

minactiveadsgrowth.description: Minimum page active-ads percent growth over activeadsgrowthperiod.
minactiveadsgrowth.allowed_values: Human percent (25 = 25%); negatives allowed for decline.

activeadsgrowthperiod.description: Lookback window for active-ads growth filter.
activeadsgrowthperiod.allowed_values: 1w, 1m, 3m. Default 1m when min/max growth set. 1w=1 week, 1m=1 month, 3m=3 months.
activeadsgrowthperiod.notes: 14d/2m exist on the dashboard but are omitted from MCP — sparse wlads baselines return empty result sets.

minpagelikes.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. Ads missing the field excluded when min set.

minadspend.description: Minimum EU ad spend total in adspendtimeframe window.
minadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier; can return upgrade JSON.

maxadspend.description: Maximum EU ad spend in window.
maxadspend.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. 999999 treated as no upper cap server-side.

adspendtimeframe.description: Rolling window ad spend is summed over (NOT a calendar month filter).

minreach.description: Minimum EU reach/views total in reachtimeframe window.
minreach.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

reachtimeframe.description: Rolling window reach is summed over.

mintraffic.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

minproductsonstore.description: Minimum published products on the Shopify store.

minprice.description: Minimum product price on landing page.

mincopylength.description: Minimum ad primary text character length.

minvideolength.description: Minimum video duration in seconds (use with mediafilter=videos).

mindays.description: Minimum days the ad has been running.
mindays.allowed_values: Integer >= 0. May require higher account tier.

from.description: Ad launch date lower bound (Meta started field — when ad began running, NOT scrape date).
from.allowed_values: YYYY-MM-DD. Requires to on same range.

to.notes: To isolate ads running in a calendar month: ad_created_to=last day of month AND fromlastseen=first day of month.

product_from.description: Shopify product creation date lower bound.

pagefrom.description: Facebook page creation date lower bound.

activestatus.description: Legacy dashboard param (no longer applied to ES queries).
activestatus.allowed_values: Ignored — use adstatus or last_seen_from/to instead.

adstatus.description: Dashboard Status filter — recently seen vs stale ads.
adstatus.allowed_values: active (lastSeen or updated_at within last 4 days), inactive (neither field within last 4 days), All/empty (no status filter).
adstatus.notes: find_winning_products forces active. Same as dashboard Status = Active.

sorting.allowed_values: relevance, datefound, mostrecent, lastseen, adspend, longestrunning, reach, adsetamount, consistency, monthlyvisits, monthlytraffic, monthlyrevenue, pageactiveads, toprank, mostsaved. Aliases: rank/top_ad/best_ranked→toprank (asc = best rank first, desc = worst rank first). ad_started→mostrecent. monthly_visits→monthlyvisits. monthly_traffic→monthlytraffic.

page.description: Pagination page index (informational). Deep pagination requires scroll from the previous response — incrementing page alone does not advance the result set.
page.allowed_values: MCP uses 1-based page (1=first page); echoed value is 0-based internal page sent to API.

scroll.description: Opaque pagination cursor. Empty/omit on the first request; pass the response scroll value on the next request with the same filters to fetch more ads. Required to download beyond the first page (especially sort_by=lastseen).
scroll.allowed_values: Opaque string from previous response; empty string or omit for first page. Stop when scroll is null/absent or data is shorter than a full page.
